chapters.title: Chapter 4: Reading the Signals as an Investor

lessons.title: Decoding the Union Budget for Portfolio Positioning

body.text: Understanding how the Budget moves markets, from Chapter 1, is analysis. Deciding what to actually do with your portfolio before, during and after it, is a separate skill, and it is the one that determines whether your macro read ever turns into a return.

children.text: Three Time Horizons, Three Different Jobs

Positioning around the Budget is not one decision, it is three, made at three different points, each answering a different question. Before the Budget, the question is what the market has already priced in. On Budget day itself, the question is what surprised, relative to that pricing, not relative to last year. In the weeks and months after, the question is whether the actual policy details, once sell-side analysts and rating agencies have fully digested them, confirm or walk back the initial market reaction.
The Pre-Budget Playbook: Positioning on Expectations

markDefs.definition: Economic Survey: an official government document, prepared by the Chief Economic Adviser's office and released a day before the Budget, reviewing the past year's economy and often signalling the government's thinking on the coming Budget's direction. It carries no legal force but is closely read as a preview.

children.text: Consensus expectations for the Budget's key numbers, from Chapter 1's five-number table, start forming weeks in advance, shaped by economist forecasts, pre-Budget consultations, and the

, released a day before the Budget itself. Sectors widely expected to benefit, infrastructure, defence, capital goods, often rally into Budget day purely on anticipation, which creates a specific risk professionals watch for closely: a Budget that delivers exactly what was expected can still see those same stocks sell off, because the good news was already in the price before the Finance Minister stood up to speak. This is the same "sell the news" dynamic that shows up around any well-telegraphed event.

India VIX, the NSE's volatility index, typically rises in the days ahead of the Budget as options markets price in the uncertainty of the announcement itself, and typically falls sharply once the Budget is out and that specific uncertainty is resolved, regardless of whether the market's reaction to the content was positive or negative.

body.title: Sizing Around Budget-Day Volatility
body.prompt: India VIX is quoted at 18 ahead of Budget day. Using the standard approximation that the expected one-day move equals the annualised implied volatility divided by the square root of 252 trading days, what is the approximate expected one-day move for Nifty, in percent? (Round to two decimal places.)
body.explanation: 18 divided by the square root of 252 (approximately 15.87) gives roughly 1.13%. This is a standard technique for translating an annualised volatility quote into a single-day expected move, useful for sizing positions or setting stop levels sensibly around a known volatility event like Budget day, rather than guessing at how large a reasonable move might be.

children.text: The Post-Budget Playbook: What Moves First

cells: 10-year G-Sec yield and Bank Nifty on NSE
Bond and bank reactions are the fastest, cleanest read on how the borrowing and deficit numbers landed relative to expectations
Sector rotation across the broader Nifty
Shows which parts of the spending and tax mix the market is repricing first, often ahead of any detailed analyst commentary
FII and DII cash flow data
Confirms whether foreign and domestic institutional money is actually following through on the initial reaction, or fading it
Sell-side target price and earnings estimate revisions
The considered view, once analysts have modelled the actual scheme, PLI or capex allocation details line by line, not just the headline

children.text: The single most useful habit from this lesson is a simple scorecard, built the moment the Budget documents are out, comparing the actual number against the pre-Budget consensus for each of the five key figures from Chapter 1, not against last year's number. A number that came in "better" than last year but worse than consensus is a negative surprise, and the market will usually treat it that way, even if headlines frame it as an improvement.

body.title: Reading a Mixed Scorecard
body.scenario: Against pre-Budget consensus: the fiscal deficit target came in slightly better than expected (a positive surprise), gross market borrowing came in worse than expected (a negative surprise, per Lesson 1's mechanic), capex allocation growth beat expectations clearly (a positive surprise), and the income tax changes were roughly in line with expectations (neutral).
body.prompt: With a mixed scorecard like this, how would you expect the market's initial reaction to differ across the bond market, banking stocks, and capital goods stocks?
body.modelAnswer: The bond market is likely to focus on the borrowing miss, the supply channel dominates near-term G-Sec yield direction regardless of the slightly better deficit percentage, so yields may drift up modestly on Budget day. Banking stocks, sensitive to both the bond move and the borrowing surprise through their G-Sec holdings, may see a muted or slightly negative initial reaction even though the headline deficit beat expectations. Capital goods and infrastructure stocks, by contrast, should react positively to the capex beat, since that is the number most directly relevant to their order book outlook, largely independent of what happened to the borrowing figure. This is exactly why a single-number reaction ("the deficit beat, so buy everything") misses how differently each part of the market actually processes a mixed scorecard.

children.text: Common Mistakes Retail Investors Make on Budget Day

columns.label: Common retail mistakes
points: Chasing headline slogans and single-stock rumours (a sector "gets a mention" and rallies, then reverses within days)
Comparing every number to last year instead of to consensus expectations
Treating Budget-day price moves as a verdict, without waiting for FII and DII flow confirmation
Sizing positions without accounting for the elevated, event-specific volatility around the day itself

columns.label: Professional approach
points: Builds a scorecard against pre-Budget consensus before reacting to any single headline
Follows the reaction sequence, bonds and banks first, sector rotation next, flows over days, estimate revisions over weeks
Waits for the multi-quarter follow-through on capex and PLI-linked announcements, which take time to show up in order books
Sizes positions with reference to India VIX and the expected move it implies, not gut feel

body.title: Sell the News, or Genuine Repricing?
body.question: A capital goods stock rallies 8% in the week before the Budget on expectations of a large capex allocation increase. On Budget day, capex allocation growth comes in exactly in line with the pre-Budget consensus. The stock falls 3% that day. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The Budget must have been bad for capital goods, since the stock fell
This is a classic "sell the news" reaction; the anticipated good news was already priced in during the pre-Budget rally, so an in-line result, not a beat, triggered some profit-booking
The stock's move is unrelated to the Budget and coincidental
In-line results should never cause a stock to fall, so this indicates a market error
body.explanation: The capex number matched expectations, it did not miss. A stock that already rallied 8% pricing in that exact outcome has little reason to rally further on confirmation alone, and some investors who bought ahead of the event often book profits once the uncertainty is resolved, regardless of whether the news itself was good. This is precisely the pre-Budget positioning risk covered earlier in this lesson, and it is a normal, recurring pattern around well-telegraphed events, not a market error.

body.title: The Budget Week Playbook
steps: The day before: read the Economic Survey for signalling, and note the street's consensus for each of the five key numbers
Budget day, first hour: track the 10-year G-Sec yield and Bank Nifty on NSE for the fastest read
Budget day, full session: watch sector rotation across the broader Nifty and build your actual-versus-consensus scorecard
The following days: check FII and DII flow data to see whether institutional money is confirming or fading the initial reaction
The following weeks: track sell-side estimate revisions as analysts model the actual scheme and allocation details, and give capex-linked order book effects several quarters before judging them

body.label: NSE India VIX and market data
body.description: Live India VIX levels, FII/DII provisional flow data, and sectoral index performance, useful for building the post-Budget scorecard described in this lesson.

body.text: Nothing in this lesson is investment advice. It describes a framework for organising Budget-day analysis, consistent with SEBI's guidelines for registered research analysts on this platform, not a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any specific security.

points: Positioning around the Budget is three separate decisions: pre-Budget expectations, Budget-day surprise, and post-Budget follow-through, each answering a different question
A Budget that matches consensus can still trigger a sell-off in stocks that rallied on anticipation, the sell-the-news pattern
The fastest, cleanest signals come first: bond yields and Bank Nifty in the first hour, sector rotation the same day, flows over days, estimate revisions over weeks
A scorecard measured against consensus expectations, not last year's numbers, is the single most useful habit for reading Budget day correctly
India VIX and its implied expected move give a concrete, calculable way to size positions sensibly around the event's elevated volatility, rather than guessing
